task: My grandmother Helen is turning 90 next Saturday and we're throwing her a family dinner at her favorite diner. Write a short card message from me, her oldest grandson, that mentions her bingo nights and her famous apple pie.
rewrite:
ambition: Skip generic "you're wonderful" praise. A strong card writer ties the bingo nights and the apple pie to what they say about Helen (the company, the luck, the care in the baking) and lets 90 years land in one plain, warm line. The voice should be the oldest grandson's, not a greeting-card verse.

agency: The rawest material is the grandson's own memories: a real bingo night, what the pie tastes like, what they call Helen. None of that is in reach. I'll use only the facts given (Helen, 90th, oldest grandson, bingo nights, famous apple pie, Saturday dinner at the favorite diner), invent no anecdotes, and leave a blank only for the sign-off name. A specific memory from the user would sharpen it most.

acceleration: Use the standard short-card shape: a direct opener, one line per detail, one line on what Helen means to the family, then a closing wish tied to the dinner. Keep it to what fits inside a card, in spoken-style sentences.

accuracy: Nothing outside the model can verify warmth. The closest proxy is reading it aloud as the grandson would say it, and checking every given detail is present and correct. Helen's reaction at the dinner is the real test.

deeper task:
Write a short card message (3 to 5 sentences) from Helen's oldest grandson for Helen's 90th birthday. The family is celebrating with a dinner next Saturday at Helen's favorite diner. It should sound like a grandson speaking, warm and plain, not like verse. Mention Helen's bingo nights and Helen's famous apple pie, each in a way that shows what it means to the family, without inventing specific anecdotes or facts I haven't given. Close with a wish for the dinner or the year ahead. Give only the card words, complete and ready to write, signed "your oldest grandson," followed by a blank for my name.

answers.plain:
Dear Grandma Helen,

Happy 90th birthday! Ninety years of love, laughter, and wisdom, and we're all lucky to be part of it.

Thank you for every bingo night that ended with you grinning and shouting "Bingo!" (and for never letting anyone forget it). And thank you for your famous apple pie. Nothing in the world tastes like home the way that pie does.

I'm so proud to be your oldest grandson, and I'm so happy to celebrate with you at your favorite diner. Here's to you, Grandma, and to many more good days ahead.

With all my love,
[Your name]
answers.nudge:
**Main card message**

Dear Grandma Helen,

Ninety years, and you still haven't lost your touch. You've been calling numbers at bingo night and winning more than your share. You've been turning out apple pies that no one else has ever matched, though plenty of us have tried. Every one of those pies tasted like home.

Thank you for all the Saturdays, the stories, and the love you've baked into this family. We're so lucky to be yours.

Happy 90th birthday. I love you more than a full house.

Your oldest grandson,
[Your name]

---

**A shorter version, if the card is small**

Grandma Helen, 90 years young and still the bingo champ with the best apple pie in the world. Thank you for everything. Happy birthday, I love you!

Your oldest grandson,
[Your name]

---

**Ways to make it yours**

- Swap in a real detail. A specific memory, like the first time you helped with the pie crust or a bingo night you went along to, will mean more to her than any line I can write.
- Use her name for you. If she has a nickname for you, sign with that instead of your name.
- Keep the handwriting. Even if you type it first, copying it out by hand makes it a keepsake.
- Mind the date. Saturday is the dinner, so if you can, give her the card at the table. People tend to keep a card that was read aloud.

If you tell me her bingo hall's name, her pie's secret ingredient, or one favorite memory, I'll rework the message around it.
